title: Leg 57 — South Pass and Oregon Buttes
subtitle: Big Sandy country, South Pass, Oregon Buttes and Lander
preflightBriefing: Welcome aboard. Today we are leaving Pinedale for a short run across one of the most important corridors in the history of the American West. We will cross the Big Sandy country, pass through the broad landscape of South Pass, swing by Oregon Buttes, then continue toward Lander and Hunt Field. Along the way there are mountain men, emigrant trails, a gold rush, women’s suffrage, a famous landmark that told wagon trains they had crossed the Continental Divide, and a landscape that in places still looks remarkably close to what nineteenth-century travelers saw. I’ll stay quiet while you taxi and depart. Once you’re airborne and settled, say Trip continue.

blocks.title: Leaving Pinedale
blocks.text: We are leaving Pinedale and the upper Green River country behind. The Wind River Range will stay prominent off the left for a while, but the route ahead opens into broad sagebrush basins that once served as corridors for trappers, emigrants and livestock drives.

blocks.title: Big Sandy country
blocks.text: The Big Sandy country ahead was more than empty space on nineteenth-century maps. Routes through this basin connected travelers with the Green River crossings and with branches of the emigrant trails. Water, grass and an easy grade could matter more than scenery when a wagon train was choosing where to go.

blocks.title: The Lander Road
blocks.text: One important later route through this region was the Lander Trail, built after Congress authorized a Pacific wagon road in the 1850s. The road stretched west from the South Pass area toward Fort Hall and cut roughly sixty miles from the older route through Fort Bridger. For emigrants moving at wagon speed, that was a meaningful saving.

blocks.title: Choosing a trail
blocks.text: It is easy to imagine the Oregon Trail as one fixed line, but travelers often faced choices between main routes and cutoffs. Those decisions balanced distance, water, road condition, livestock forage and reports from people coming the other way. A shortcut on paper could become a very bad bargain if the terrain or water supply disappointed.

blocks.title: Approaching South Pass country
blocks.text: We are heading into South Pass country now. What makes the pass remarkable is how unremarkable it can look. Instead of a dramatic notch between cliffs, it is a broad, gentle opening in the Continental Divide, exactly the quality that made it so useful to wagons.

blocks.title: The Astorians and the pass
blocks.text: European-American knowledge of South Pass is usually traced to the Astorian expedition. Robert Stuart’s returning party crossed this country in 1812 after learning of the route from Native people. The information did not immediately transform western travel, but fur trappers rediscovered the pass in the 1820s and its importance became impossible to miss.

blocks.title: Gateway to the continent
blocks.text: Between about 1840 and 1869, the National Park Service estimates that roughly half a million overland emigrants crossed South Pass on routes toward Oregon, California, Utah and other western destinations. Its gentle grade allowed wagons, handcarts, stagecoaches, the Pony Express and eventually telegraph lines to cross the Continental Divide through the same broad corridor.

blocks.title: Two women at South Pass
blocks.text: In 1836, missionaries Narcissa Whitman and Eliza Spalding became the first white women known to cross South Pass. Their journey became part of the proof, in the minds of many Americans, that families as well as fur trappers and explorers could travel overland into the far West.

blocks.title: South Pass in view
blocks.text: South Pass is spread across the open country ahead and to the right. The historic crossing itself sits at about seventy-four hundred feet. From the air, the scale is the story: this is less a mountain notch than a wide, forgiving saddle through the Rockies.

blocks.title: Oregon Buttes ahead
blocks.text: Oregon Buttes should now stand out ahead-right as isolated high ground above the sagebrush. To westbound emigrants they were a major visual landmark, often called the Table Rocks, and could dominate the horizon for a day’s travel or more.

blocks.title: A landmark with a political meaning
blocks.text: The name carried extra meaning for early travelers. The buttes stood just beyond South Pass, so reaching them symbolized entry into the Oregon country at a time when the Pacific Northwest was still being contested and then divided between the United States and Britain. One emigrant in 1843 wrote that the party had entered the land of promise.

blocks.title: An island in the Red Desert
blocks.text: The buttes rise to about eighty-six hundred feet and form a striking island of higher ground in the northwestern Red Desert. BLM describes a surprisingly varied mix of limber pine, aspen and wet meadows around them, along with good raptor habitat and enormous views across the surrounding basin.

blocks.title: Gold near South Pass
blocks.text: The emigrant era was not the end of South Pass history. A gold rush took off in the late 1860s after rich ore was reported near what became the Carissa Mine. South Pass City grew rapidly, with mills, businesses and prospectors chasing hundreds of claims, then declined almost as quickly when many of those hopes failed to pay out.

blocks.title: South Pass City and women’s suffrage
blocks.text: South Pass City also became tied to one of Wyoming’s most famous political stories. Saloonkeeper and legislator William Bright introduced the 1869 bill that made Wyoming Territory the first government to guarantee women the right to vote. Soon afterward, Esther Hobart Morris served there as justice of the peace, becoming the first woman in the United States to hold judicial office.

blocks.title: A boomtown preserved
blocks.text: Today South Pass City survives as a state historic site with more than twenty original buildings restored or preserved. The old town, the Carissa Mine and the surrounding trail landscape make this one of the rare places where the emigrant story, mining story and early Wyoming politics all overlap in the same small area.

blocks.title: Lander ahead
blocks.text: Lander is ahead now, tucked against the eastern side of the Wind River Range. The town grew as a regional center for ranching, mining and travel, and its name is a reminder of Frederick W. Lander, the engineer associated with the wagon road we discussed earlier.

blocks.title: A modern mountain gateway
blocks.text: Modern Lander has built a strong outdoor identity around climbing, hiking and access to the Wind River Mountains. Sinks Canyon, just south of town, is one of the best-known nearby attractions, where the Popo Agie River disappears into a limestone cavern and reappears farther down the canyon.

blocks.title: Hunt Field
blocks.text: Hunt Field is just ahead on the east side of Lander. We have crossed only about sixty-six nautical miles today, but that short stretch covered one of the great overland gateways of the nineteenth-century American West.
